title: Nest‐box supplementation can amplify intraspecific exploitation: RFID reveals frequent nest switching and lower fledging success in barn owls
content:
High breeding density in nest box-based biological control programs can unintentionally increase intraspecific exploitation, reducing fledging success even when apparent reproductive output remains high. Management evaluations should move beyond occupancy and fledgling counts to include individual-level performance metrics, such as fledging success. Where possible, nest-box programs should avoid extreme local clustering of simultaneously active broods and monitor high-density breeding systems for density-dependent interactions that can undermine long-term effectiveness.

Abstract

Nest-box supplementation is widely used to increase populations of barn owls (Tyto alba) for environmentally friendly rodent control in agricultural landscapes. Program effectiveness is typically evaluated using coarse metrics such as nest occupancy or fledgling counts, which may overlook density-dependent processes that reduce individual survival and recruitment. We used continuous radio-frequency identification (RFID) monitoring to test whether high breeding density in a nest-box network promotes nest switching by fledglings and is associated with reduced fledging success in host broods. Across two breeding seasons (2020–2021), we PIT-tagged 464 nestlings and 108 adults and monitored 50 active nest boxes, recording over 1.2 million individual detections. Nest switching was common: 12.9% of tagged fledglings visited foreign nests, and 54% of monitored nest boxes were visited by at least one nest switcher. Nest-switcher rate increased with local nest-box density and decreased with host brood age but was unrelated to female provisioning, measured as parental prey-delivery rate. The number of fledglings produced per nest was not associated with nest-switching rate. By contrast, fledging success declined with increasing nest-switcher rate, indicating a negative association that was not detected by brood size or fledgling counts alone. Synthesis and applications: High breeding density in nest box-based biological control programs can unintentionally increase intraspecific exploitation, reducing fledging success even when apparent reproductive output remains high. Management evaluations should move beyond occupancy and fledgling counts to include individual-level performance metrics, such as fledging success. Where possible, nest-box programs should avoid extreme local clustering of simultaneously active broods and monitor high-density breeding systems for density-dependent interactions that can undermine long-term effectiveness.
